los.text: Identify the concept of flow-through of passive income and loss as it applies to DPPs.
Differentiate between the roles of the general partner(s) and the limited partner(s) in a DPP.
Recognize the characteristics of the pooled investment vehicles that are considered alternative investments.
Compare viaticals and life settlement policies. (Book: no longer tested.)
Contrast passive and active real estate investing. (Book: no longer tested.)
Identify the different types of commodities and precious metals that are popular investments.
Explain the benefits and risks of alternative investments in client portfolios.
Digital assets (book addendum not in PDF — supplemented from NASAA sources).

concepts.explanation: Direct participation programs (DPPs) — most are limited partnerships (real estate LPs, oil and gas programs, movie productions) — let the economic results of a business flow directly through to investors: income, gains, losses, deductions and credits, with no corporate-level tax and no dividends. Because the investor takes no part in management, the income and losses are passive, and passive losses can be deducted only against passive income. Limited partners have limited liability: creditors cannot reach them personally; the most they can lose is what they invested plus any committed but unpaid amounts. Ownership units are called interests, not shares. Unlike a REIT, a DPP passes through losses as well as income.
rules: Flow-through of income AND loss; passive losses offset only passive income.
LP max loss = investment + unpaid commitments.
DPP vs. REIT: REIT distributes ≥90% of income but never passes through losses.
examples: A RELP's loss can offset income from another DPP, not the investor's salary.
misconceptions: Thinking a DPP pays dividends or that its losses offset ordinary income.

concepts.subtopic: General partner vs. limited partner; evaluating and buying a DPP
concepts.explanation: Every limited partnership needs at least one general partner (management) and one limited partner (capital). The GP makes binding decisions, buys/sells/manages property and money, supervises the business, keeps at least a 1% financial interest, and has unlimited personal liability. The GP is a fiduciary to the LPs: no borrowing from the partnership, no competing with it, no commingling funds, and generally no profit distributions until LPs are paid. LPs are passive — no management or day-to-day decisions; an LP who takes an active role risks losing limited liability. LPs receive cash distributions and gains; total yield counts tax deductions, distributions and gains. Choose a program that is economically viable, whose tax benefits the investor can use, whose GP has a track record, whose objectives and time frame match the investor's, and whose costs/revenues are in line with similar ventures. A program that is a tax dodge without economic purpose is an abusive tax shelter (IRS disallows deductions, assesses back taxes, interest, penalties). DPPs are illiquid; even public ones often need GP approval to sell. Offered privately (exempt) or publicly registered; investors sign a subscription agreement (net worth, income, power of attorney naming the GP), and the selling agent must verify it is complete and accurate.
rules: Management is always the GP's; LPs who manage jeopardize limited liability.
GP: unlimited liability, ≥1% interest, fiduciary duties.
Subscription agreement required; agent checks accuracy.
examples: An investor wanting current passive income should avoid an exploratory oil and gas program (low success rate, years to income).
misconceptions: Putting management in the hands of an investor committee.

concepts.explanation: ETNs register under the Securities Act of 1933 as debt securities (ETFs register under the 1940 Act as investment companies). An ETN is unsecured exchange-traded debt whose return is linked to an index or benchmark instead of paying periodic interest; 'equity-linked notes' (ELNs) are a misnomer — they are debt. The issuer publishes a daily indicative value and issues or redeems notes to keep the price near it (a potential conflict of interest). ETNs do not hold the underlying assets. Risks: credit risk (unsecured obligation of the issuer), market risk, liquidity risk (a market may not develop), call/early-redemption/acceleration risk at the issuer's discretion, and conflicts of interest (the issuer may trade against note holders). Suitable only for knowledgeable investors; FINRA calls ELNs nonconventional structured investments.
rules: ETN = debt (1933 Act); ETF = investment company (1940 Act).
ETN risks: credit, market, liquidity, call, conflicts.
misconceptions: Treating an ELN/ETN as an equity security.

concepts.subtopic: Leveraged and inverse funds; structured products
concepts.explanation: Leveraged funds aim for a multiple (2×, 3×) of an index's return; no rule limits the leverage; they use options, futures and swaps, so losses are magnified by the same multiple. Inverse (short/bear) funds aim for the opposite of the index (index −2% → fund +2%), and can also be leveraged. Most leveraged and inverse ETFs reset daily — they target the daily result — so over weeks or months performance can differ dramatically from the index; FINRA warns they are unsuitable for buy-and-hold investors or anyone without a very short horizon (one 2× VIX ETN's prospectus said its long-term expected value is zero). Exchange-traded versions trade intraday at supply-and-demand prices and can be margined; non-exchange versions (inverse mutual funds) are priced and redeemed like any fund. No guarantee of meeting objectives. Structured products are built to meet specific needs, often restructuring debt so the issuer borrows more cheaply while investors get features (derivatives, possible principal protection); highly complex, for sophisticated investors, can add diversification. A structured note with principal protection (FINRA) combines a bond — typically a zero-coupon — with a derivative whose payoff tracks an asset or index, promising full or partial return of principal at maturity; the promise is only as good as the issuer (Lehman Brothers' notes, 2008).
rules: Leveraged/inverse ETFs: daily reset → short-term tools only.
Principal protection = issuer's promise = credit risk.
examples: 3× inverse S&P fund: index −1% in a day → fund +3%.
misconceptions: Recommending an inverse ETF to a long-horizon investor.

concepts.explanation: Book flags LO 5.d as no longer tested on the Series 65; kept for completeness. Viatical settlement: sale of a life policy by someone terminally ill with a life expectancy of 24 months or less, any age. Life settlement: seller generally 65+, in decent health, life expectancy of 2 to 10+ years. In both, the seller gets more than cash surrender value but less than the death benefit; investors buy the policy, keep paying premiums, and collect the death benefit. NASAA treats these as securities (registration and antifraud provisions apply); licensing varies by state. Risks to the investor: no secondary market (hard to value), insured outlives expectancy (lower return), insurer failure, and the moral discomfort of profiting from a death.
rules: Viatical: ≤24-month life expectancy, terminal. Life settlement: 65+, healthy, ≥2 years.
examples: A healthy 68-year-old who no longer needs a $1 million whole life policy → life settlement, not viatical.

concepts.subtopic: Passive vs. active real estate investing
concepts.explanation: Book flags LO 5.e as no longer tested. Passive real estate investing: others do the work — REITs, real estate limited partnerships, stock in home builders. Active: the investor finds tenants, collects rent, repairs, flips. Taxation: RELP income is passive (ordinary rates) and passive losses offset only passive income; an active investor flipping homes as a business may deduct losses against ordinary income.
rules: Passive = REIT, RELP, real estate company stock. Active = managing/flipping property yourself.

concepts.subtopic: Types of commodities; how to invest; precious vs. industrial metals
concepts.explanation: Investors reach commodities directly through futures (forwards are for producers and industrial users) or indirectly through exchange-traded products tracking a commodity index and mutual funds owning commodity-related businesses (an energy fund owns exploration, refining and distribution stocks). Agricultural commodities (corn, wheat, oats, soybeans) and animal products (beef, pork, eggs) remain active; crude oil is the most traded commodity today, coffee often second; frozen orange juice is a classic. Industrial metals — aluminum, nickel, copper, lead — are NOT precious metals. Precious metals for the exam: gold, silver, platinum (think jewelry store or airline status tiers) — the traditional store of wealth and inflation hedge. Rising demand for a metal argues for owning the producers (e.g., copper miners), not selling its futures.
rules: Precious: gold, silver, platinum. Industrial: aluminum, nickel, copper, lead, tin.
Direct = futures; indirect = commodity ETPs or sector funds.
exceptions: Diamonds are precious but not metals.
misconceptions: Choosing lead, cadmium or uranium as an inflation-hedge precious metal.

concepts.subtopic: Alts in general; DPP benefits and risks
concepts.explanation: Most alternatives share low or negative correlation with stocks (more diversification, potentially higher long-term return at lower risk) and the chance of abnormal returns — high or low. DPP advantages: managed by others, flow-through of income and certain expenses, limited liability. DPP disadvantages (exam focus): liquidity risk (the greatest — limited secondary market), legislative risk (tax-law changes strip assumed benefits while the investor is locked in), audit risk (DPP ownership raises the odds of an IRS audit), and depreciation recapture (depreciation lowers basis; gain on sale above basis is recaptured and taxed, possibly at ordinary rates). Program-specific risks too — a dry hole in an oil and gas drilling program.
rules: DPP benefits: management by others, flow-through, limited liability.
DPP risks: illiquidity (#1), legislative, audit, depreciation recapture.
misconceptions: Listing 'high liquidity' or 'immunity from audit' as DPP benefits — both are the opposite.

concepts.subtopic: Commodities, precious metals, real estate, structured products
concepts.explanation: Commodities: benefits — inflation hedge, diversification (uncorrelated with stocks), potential returns from global supply/demand; risks — extreme price volatility (principal risk), foreign-market risks, leverage working against you, and no income ever (gold pays no dividend; only capital gains). A good asset allocation includes some commodity exposure (Unit 21). Precious metals add storage costs and wide bid-ask spreads. Real estate: leverage can boost returns, possible tax advantages, appreciation, and low correlation with stocks (not high). Structured products: little or no liquidity (customized), returns realized only at maturity (buy-and-hold, not traders), issuer credit risk, and inefficient pricing (market price may not reflect real value → abnormal returns either way).
rules: Commodities give no income — only capital gains.
Structured products: illiquid, hold to maturity, credit risk, pricing inefficiency.
examples: Report says copper demand will double → buy copper mining companies, not sell copper futures.
misconceptions: Citing a high correlation with stocks as a reason to own real estate.

concepts.subtopic: Cryptocurrencies and tokens: what they are and their risks
concepts.explanation: EXTERNAL SUPPLEMENT (NASAA Informed Investor Advisory on Cryptocurrencies; NASAA 2023 outline lists digital assets under 'other assets'). Digital assets such as cryptocurrencies are intangible virtual coins or tokens that exist only online, recorded on a distributed ledger (blockchain). They are not issued, backed or insured by any government or central bank, are not legal tender, are not covered by FDIC or SIPC insurance, and often cannot be freely exchanged for fiat currency. Holders control them through a digital wallet and a private key — lose the key or get hacked and the asset is usually unrecoverable. Issuers may raise money through initial coin/token offerings (ICOs/ITOs), which are not stock and may be unregistered securities; many trade on lightly regulated or opaque exchanges where true value is hard to verify. NASAA calls crypto investing 'extremely risky speculation with a high risk of loss': extreme volatility (unsuitable for most long-term savings or retirement goals), custody/cyber risk, fraud (fake wallets, pump-and-dump, Ponzi-style and MLM schemes, aggressive social-media promotion), and regulatory uncertainty. For advisers: treat recommendations as speculative, document suitability carefully, be alert to scams, and consider the investor's ability to bear total loss.
rules: Not government-backed, not insured (no FDIC/SIPC), not legal tender.
Private key = control; loss or hack usually unrecoverable.
Suitability: speculative; investor must be able to lose everything.
exceptions: Some crypto products (e.g., exchange-traded products that hold or track bitcoin) are registered securities and trade on exchanges — still volatile, but with securities-law disclosure.
misconceptions: Assuming a crypto account at an exchange is insured like a bank or brokerage account.

lessons.title: Direct participation programs: who runs it, who funds it, who is liable
lessons.objective: Explain flow-through and passive income/loss, distinguish general and limited partners, and describe how DPPs are evaluated and purchased.

blocks.b:
A **direct participation program** (DPP) is simply another way to own a business — usually a **limited partnership**: a real estate LP, an oil and gas drilling program, a film production. Instead of paying corporate tax and dividends, the partnership **passes income, gains, losses, deductions and credits straight through** to investors.

Because investors take no part in running it, everything they receive is **passive**: passive income is taxed as ordinary income, and **passive losses can be deducted only against passive income** (from other DPPs) — never against salary.

**Limited liability**: creditors can't come after a limited partner personally. The most an LP can lose is the amount invested **plus any committed but unpaid funds**. Units are called **interests**, not shares.

Contrast with a REIT: a REIT distributes 90%+ of its income, but it never passes through **losses**; a DPP passes through both.

Every DPP needs **at least one GP and one LP**.

**General partner** — management. Makes decisions that bind the partnership, buys/sells and manages property and money, supervises everything, keeps at least a **1% financial interest**, and bears **unlimited personal liability**. The GP is a **fiduciary** to the LPs: no borrowing from the partnership, no competing with it, no commingling funds, and generally **no profit distributions until the LPs have been paid**.

**Limited partner** — capital. Passive: no management, no day-to-day decisions. An LP who starts managing **risks losing limited liability**. LPs receive cash distributions and gains; total yield counts tax deductions, distributions and gains.

'Management is **always** in the hands of the GP' — one of the few places where *always* is right.

Invest in a DPP because it is **economically viable**, you can **use the tax benefits**, the GP has a **track record** with similar programs, its **objectives and time frame match yours**, and its costs and revenues are in line with similar ventures. A program built purely as a tax dodge with no economic purpose is an **abusive tax shelter** — the IRS disallows deductions and assesses back taxes, interest and penalties.

Match objectives: someone who wants **current passive income** should not buy an **exploratory** oil and gas program — most wells are dry, and even a hit takes years to pay.

DPPs are **illiquid**: most are private placements, and even publicly traded ones often need the GP's approval before you can sell.

Offered as **private placements** (exempt from registration) or **publicly registered**. Either way the investor signs a **subscription agreement** stating net worth and income and granting a power of attorney naming the GP as agent; the **selling agent** must make sure it is complete and accurate.

lessons.title: ETNs, leveraged and inverse funds, structured products
lessons.objective: Distinguish ETNs from ETFs and list ETN risks; explain daily-reset leveraged and inverse funds and their suitability; describe structured products and principal-protected notes.

blocks.b:
ETNs are **cousins** of ETFs with one structural difference that drives everything: an **ETN registers under the Securities Act of 1933 as a debt security**; an **ETF registers under the Investment Company Act of 1940**. An ETN is **unsecured** exchange-traded debt whose return is **linked to an index** instead of paying periodic interest. Some are called **equity-linked notes (ELNs)** — a misnomer, since they are debt.

The issuer publishes a daily **indicative value** and issues or redeems notes to keep the market price near it — note the **conflict of interest**, since the issuer controls that process. ETNs **do not hold the underlying assets**.

**Risks**: **credit risk** (unsecured promise of the issuer), market risk, **liquidity risk** (a market may never develop), **call/early-redemption/acceleration** at the issuer's discretion, and **conflicts of interest** (the issuer may trade against holders). Only for investors who understand the risks; FINRA calls ELNs nonconventional structured investments.

**Leveraged** funds seek a **multiple** of an index's return (2×, 3×); no rule caps the leverage, and they use options, futures and swaps — so a falling index loses you 2× or 3× as much. **Inverse** (short, bear) funds seek the **opposite** of the index (index −2% → fund +2%) and can be leveraged too.

The trap: most leveraged and inverse ETFs **reset daily** — they target the **daily** result. Over weeks or months, returns can diverge wildly from the index (or its inverse). FINRA's warning: unsuitable for **buy-and-hold** investors or anyone without a **very short time horizon**. One 2× VIX ETN's own prospectus: 'The long-term expected value of your ETNs is zero.'

Exchange-traded versions trade intraday at supply-and-demand prices and can be margined; inverse **mutual funds** are priced and redeemed like any fund. Neither guarantees it will hit its objective.

Built to meet a specific need — often a debt issue restructured so the issuer borrows **more cheaply** while investors accept the lower rate in exchange for **features** (derivatives, possible principal protection). Highly complex; for **sophisticated** investors; can add diversification.

A **structured note with principal protection** (FINRA's definition) combines a bond — usually a **zero-coupon** — with a derivative whose payoff tracks an asset, index or benchmark, promising full or partial return of principal at maturity. That promise is **only as good as the issuer**: holders of Lehman Brothers' principal-protected notes found that out in September 2008.

lessons.title: Commodities and precious metals (plus two retired topics)
lessons.objective: Identify commodity types, direct vs. indirect ways to invest, and which metals count as precious; briefly recognize viaticals vs. life settlements and passive vs. active real estate (no longer tested).

blocks.b:
**Direct** exposure comes through **futures** (forwards are for producers and industrial users). **Indirect** exposure: **exchange-traded products** that follow a commodity index, or **mutual funds** that own commodity-related companies (an energy fund holds exploration, refining, storage and distribution stocks).

What trades: **agricultural** products (corn, wheat, oats, soybeans), **animal** products (beef, pork, eggs), the famous **frozen orange juice** contract — and today the most-traded commodity is **crude oil**, with coffee often second.

**Industrial metals** — aluminum, nickel, copper, lead, tin — are **not precious**. **Precious metals** for the exam: **gold, silver, platinum** (think jewelry store, or airline status tiers). They have stored wealth for millennia and are the classic **inflation hedge**.

If a report says industrial demand for copper will double, the play is to **buy copper mining companies**, not sell copper futures.

blocks.h: Two topics the book says are no longer tested
blocks.b:
Kaplan flags LO 5.d and 5.e as removed from the Series 65. Know them lightly.

**Viatical vs. life settlement** — both sell a life policy to an investor for more than cash value but less than the death benefit; the buyer keeps paying premiums and collects at death. **Viatical**: terminally ill, life expectancy **24 months or less**, any age. **Life settlement**: generally **65+**, in decent health, expectancy **2 to 10+ years**. NASAA treats both as **securities**. Investor risks: no secondary market (hard to value), insured outlives expectancy, insurer failure, and the moral discomfort.

**Passive vs. active real estate** — passive means others do the work: **REITs, RELPs, stock in home builders**. Active means you find tenants, collect rent, fix things or flip. RELP income is passive (ordinary rates) and its losses offset only passive income; a flipper running a business may deduct losses against ordinary income.

lessons.title: Benefits and risks of alternatives
lessons.objective: State the general case for alternatives and the specific benefits and risks of DPPs, commodities and precious metals, real estate, and structured products.

blocks.b: Most alts have **low or negative correlation** with the stock market, so adding them **diversifies** the portfolio — potentially higher long-term return at lower risk. They also bring the chance of **abnormal returns, high and low**. Suitability is case by case: objectives, circumstances, sophistication.

**Benefits**: managed by others; **flow-through** of income and certain expenses; **limited liability** (investment plus unpaid commitments).

**Risks** (the exam's favorite part):
- **Liquidity risk** — the greatest disadvantage; there is barely a secondary market.
- **Legislative risk** — Congress changes the tax law and the assumed benefits vanish while you are locked in.
- **Audit risk** — owning a DPP raises the odds the IRS audits your return.
- **Depreciation recapture** — depreciation lowers the asset's basis; sell above basis and the excess is recaptured and taxed, possibly at ordinary rates.
- Program-specific risk — the **dry hole** in a drilling program.

Not benefits: high liquidity, immunity from audit.

blocks.h: Commodities, metals, real estate, structured products
blocks.b:
**Commodities** — for: **inflation hedge**, **diversification** (uncorrelated with stocks), returns from global supply and demand. Against: **extreme volatility**, foreign-market risks, **leverage** in a downturn, and **no income — ever**. Gold pays no dividend; the only return is a capital gain. A sound asset allocation still includes some commodity exposure.

**Precious metals** add **storage costs** and **wide bid-ask spreads** on top of the lack of income.

**Real estate** — reasons to own: **leverage** can amplify returns, possible **tax advantages**, **appreciation**, and **low** correlation with stocks (a *high* correlation would be a reason not to).

**Structured products** — risks: **little or no liquidity** (customized), returns realized only **at maturity** (buy-and-hold, not traders), issuer **credit risk**, and **inefficient pricing** — market price may not reflect real value, producing abnormal returns in either direction.

lessons.title: Digital assets (supplement)
lessons.objective: Describe what cryptocurrencies and tokens are, how they are held, and the risks NASAA warns investors about.

blocks.b: Your book's LO 5.h lives in a Kaplan **Addendum** that is not in the PDF. This lesson is built from **NASAA's Informed Investor Advisory on Cryptocurrencies** and the NASAA 2023 outline, which lists **digital assets** under 'other assets.' Facts here are labeled external in every question.

Cryptocurrencies and tokens are **intangible digital assets** that exist only online, recorded on a **distributed ledger (blockchain)**. Anyone can create one. They are **not issued, backed, controlled or insured** by any government or central bank, are **not legal tender**, are **not covered by FDIC or SIPC** insurance, and often **cannot be freely exchanged** for dollars.

You hold them in a **digital wallet** and control them with a **private key**. Lose the key, or get hacked, and the asset is usually **gone for good** — losses are hard to trace, especially with overseas issuers.

Issuers may raise money through **initial coin offerings / initial token offerings (ICOs/ITOs)**. These are **not stock**, and many are **unregistered securities** sold without investor protections. Trading often happens on **lightly regulated, opaque exchanges** where true value is hard to verify. (Registered exchange-traded products that hold or track bitcoin exist — they carry securities-law disclosure but the same price volatility.)

NASAA's summary: crypto investing is **'extremely risky speculation with a high risk of loss'** — be prepared to lose the entire investment.
- **Volatility** — swings make them unsuitable for most long-term savings or retirement goals.
- **No insurance** — no deposit or securities insurance.
- **No central authority / regulatory uncertainty** — they don't fit neatly in existing rules, so many protections are missing.
- **Custody and cyber risk** — hacks, malicious wallet software, weak security; recovery often impossible.
- **Fraud** — fake wallets that steal keys, pump-and-dump on thin coins, Ponzi-style and multi-level marketing schemes promising high low-risk returns, aggressive social-media promotion.

For an adviser: treat any recommendation as **speculative**, document suitability and the client's capacity to absorb a **total loss**, and check with the state regulator about unregistered offerings.

questions.stem: An investor in a real estate limited partnership receives an allocation of the partnership's net loss for the year. Under the passive activity rules, that loss may be deducted against
options: the investor's salary.
passive income from other partnerships.
interest and dividends.
any ordinary income up to $25,000.
questions.explanation: Income and loss from a DPP are passive because the LP takes no part in management; passive losses offset only passive income.
why: Interest and dividends are portfolio income, not passive.
The passive rules do not allow a general ordinary-income offset.

questions.stem: A difference between a real estate limited partnership (RELP) and a REIT is that
options: the RELP pays dividends while the REIT does not.
the RELP passes through both income and losses, while the REIT passes through income but not losses.
the REIT is less liquid than the RELP.
only the RELP must distribute 90% of its income.
questions.explanation: DPPs are full flow-through vehicles; REITs distribute at least 90% of taxable income as dividends but keep losses at the trust level. Publicly traded REITs are far more liquid than partnership interests.
why: Partnerships make distributions, not dividends; REITs pay dividends.
REITs trade on exchanges; DPPs are illiquid.

questions.stem: In a limited partnership, personal liability for the debts of the business rests with
options: the limited partners.
the general partner(s).
the subscription agent.
all partners equally.
questions.explanation: General partners manage the business and bear unlimited personal liability; limited partners can lose only their investment plus unpaid commitments.
why: The selling agent has no liability for partnership debts.

questions.stem: Which statement about the parties to a direct participation program is correct?
options: Limited partners manage the enterprise through an elected committee.
A general partner must maintain at least a 1% financial interest and may not borrow from or compete with the partnership.
A limited partner who takes an active management role gains additional liability protection.
General partners are paid their share of profits before limited partners receive distributions.
questions.explanation: GPs run the business, keep at least a 1% interest, and owe fiduciary duties (no borrowing, competing or commingling); they generally receive distributions only after LPs. An LP who manages risks losing limited liability.
why: Management belongs solely to the GP.
Active involvement endangers an LP's limited liability.

questions.stem: A client wants a DPP that will produce current passive income within the next year. Which program is LEAST appropriate?
options: An existing-property real estate program with established tenants
An equipment leasing program with leases in place
An exploratory oil and gas drilling program
An income-producing oil and gas program buying producing wells
questions.explanation: Exploratory drilling programs have low success rates and, even when successful, take years to generate income — the opposite of the client's objective.
why: Leases in place produce current income.

questions.stem: The principal structural difference between an exchange-traded note (ETN) and an exchange-traded fund (ETF) is that
options: the ETN registers under the Investment Company Act of 1940 while the ETF registers under the Securities Act of 1933.
the ETN is an unsecured debt security of its issuer while the ETF is an investment company that holds the underlying assets.
ETNs pay periodic interest while ETFs do not.
ETNs cannot be traded on an exchange.
questions.explanation: ETNs are debt instruments registered under the 1933 Act whose return is linked to an index; they do not hold the underlying assets. ETFs are 1940 Act investment companies.
why: ETNs pay an index-linked return, not periodic interest.

questions.stem: An investor in an ETN is exposed to all of the following risks EXCEPT
options: the credit risk of the issuer.
the issuer calling the notes early.
the risk that the issuer's own trading conflicts with note holders' interests.
the risk of losing limited partner status.
questions.explanation: ETN risks include credit, market, liquidity, call/early redemption, and conflicts of interest. Limited partner status is a DPP concept.
why: ETNs may be called at the issuer's discretion.
The issuer may short or otherwise trade against holders.

questions.stem: A retiree with a 15-year horizon asks whether to put a portion of her IRA in a 3× inverse S&P 500 ETF as a 'permanent hedge.' The adviser should explain that such funds
options: are designed to achieve their objective daily and can diverge greatly from the index over long periods, making them unsuitable for buy-and-hold investors.
are guaranteed to rise 3% for every 1% the index falls over any holding period.
cannot be held in a retirement account.
pay a fixed dividend that offsets index losses.
questions.explanation: Leveraged and inverse ETFs reset daily; FINRA warns their long-term performance can differ dramatically from the index, so they suit only very short horizons.
why: The multiple applies to daily returns and nothing is guaranteed.
Account type is not the issue; suitability is.

questions.stem: On a day when its benchmark index falls 2%, a 2× inverse ETF tracking that index would be expected to
options: fall 4%.
fall 2%.
rise 2%.
rise 4%.
questions.explanation: Inverse means opposite; 2× doubles it: −2% index → +4% fund (for that day).
why: That would be a 2× leveraged (long) fund.
That would be an unleveraged long index fund.

questions.stem: A structured note with principal protection typically combines
options: a zero-coupon bond with a derivative linked to an index, with the principal guarantee depending on the issuer's creditworthiness.
common stock with a put option guaranteed by the OCC.
a Treasury bond with FDIC insurance.
a limited partnership interest with a futures contract.
questions.explanation: FINRA describes these as a bond (usually a zero) plus a derivative whose payoff tracks an asset or index; the promise of principal is only as good as the issuer — Lehman's 2008 bankruptcy proved the point.
why: The OCC guarantees listed options, not structured notes.
There is no FDIC insurance on structured products.

questions.stem: (Book: no longer tested.) A 70-year-old in good health no longer needs a $500,000 permanent life policy and wants to receive more than its cash surrender value. The appropriate transaction is
options: a viatical settlement.
a life settlement.
a policy loan.
a 1035 exchange into an annuity.
questions.explanation: Life settlements are for insureds generally 65+ with a life expectancy of at least 2 years; viaticals require a terminal illness with 24 months or less to live.
why: A loan keeps a policy that is no longer wanted.
An exchange does not deliver cash above surrender value.

questions.stem: (Book: no longer tested.) Which of the following is an ACTIVE real estate investment?
options: Shares of a mortgage REIT
Units of a real estate limited partnership
Buying duplexes and managing their rental yourself
Common stock of a home-building company
questions.explanation: Active investing means the investor does the work — finding tenants, collecting rent, repairs. REITs, RELPs and real estate stocks are passive.
why: Passive — the REIT does the work.

questions.stem: An investor seeking precious metals as an inflation hedge would most likely purchase
options: copper.
aluminum.
platinum.
nickel.
questions.explanation: Gold, silver and platinum are the precious metals; copper, aluminum, nickel and lead are industrial metals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an INDIRECT way for an individual investor to gain exposure to commodities?
options: Buying crude oil futures contracts
Buying a mutual fund that owns energy exploration and refining companies
Entering a forward contract for soybeans
Taking physical delivery of gold bullion
questions.explanation: Futures, forwards and physical ownership are direct; funds owning commodity-related businesses and index-tracking ETPs are indirect.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are benefits of investing in a direct participation program?
I. High liquidity
II. Flow-through of operating losses
III. Limited liability
IV. Reduced likelihood of an IRS audit
options: I and II
II and III
I and IV
III and IV
questions.explanation: DPPs pass through losses (usable against passive income) and limit liability to the investment. They are illiquid and actually raise audit risk.
why: Both are the opposite of DPP characteristics.

questions.stem: When a DPP sells a depreciated asset for more than its adjusted basis, the excess may be taxed at ordinary income rates. This is known as
options: legislative risk.
depreciation recapture.
a passive loss carryforward.
phantom income.
questions.explanation: Depreciation lowers basis; gain above that basis on sale is 'recaptured' and taxed, possibly as ordinary income.
why: Legislative risk is the risk of tax-law changes.
Phantom income is taxable income not received in cash (e.g., zero-coupon accretion).

questions.stem: A disadvantage shared by gold, silver and other commodity investments is that they
options: are highly correlated with stock returns.
provide no current income.
cannot be used to hedge inflation.
are exempt from price volatility.
questions.explanation: Commodities never pay interest or dividends — the only return is a capital gain. They are uncorrelated with stocks, serve as inflation hedges, and are highly volatile.
why: They are generally uncorrelated with stocks.
Inflation hedging is a key benefit.

questions.stem: All of the following are risks of structured products EXCEPT
options: little or no liquidity.
returns that are generally not realized until maturity.
credit risk of the issuing institution.
mandatory daily resets of leverage.
questions.explanation: Structured products are illiquid, mature-dependent, and subject to issuer credit risk and inefficient pricing. Daily resets characterize leveraged/inverse ETFs.

questions.stem: Reasons an investor might add real estate to a portfolio include all of the following EXCEPT
options: potential appreciation.
possible tax advantages.
a high correlation with stock market returns.
the ability to increase returns through leverage.
questions.explanation: Real estate's appeal includes its LOW correlation with stocks, which improves diversification; a high correlation would be a drawback.
why: Mortgage financing lets investors leverage returns.

questions.source: external: NASAA Informed Investor Advisory — Cryptocurrencies
questions.stem: Which statement about cryptocurrencies held in an account at an online crypto exchange is correct?
options: Balances are insured by the FDIC up to $250,000.
Balances are protected by SIPC like a brokerage account.
They are not backed or insured by any government, and losses from hacking may be unrecoverable.
They are legal tender that the exchange must convert to dollars on demand.
questions.explanation: NASAA stresses that digital assets are not government-backed or insured, custody and cyber losses are often unrecoverable, and conversion to fiat is not assured.
why: Cryptocurrencies are not legal tender and conversion is not guaranteed.

questions.source: external: NASAA Informed Investor Advisory — Cryptocurrencies
questions.stem: A client receives a social-media message promoting a new token offering that promises 20% monthly returns with 'no risk.' The IAR's most appropriate response is to
options: recommend a small allocation because the upside is large.
explain that such promises are classic warning signs of fraud and that ICOs may be unregistered securities offered without investor protections.
confirm that the offering is safe because tokens are not securities.
suggest the client fund the purchase from retirement savings to defer taxes.
questions.explanation: Promises of high, low-risk returns and aggressive social-media promotion are red flags in NASAA's advisory; unregistered ICOs/ITOs lack the protections of registered offerings.
why: Promised risk-free high returns are a fraud indicator, not an opportunity.
Tokens can be securities, and 'safe' cannot be assumed.
Retirement funds are the last place for speculative, fraud-prone products.

questions.source: external: NASAA Informed Investor Advisory — Cryptocurrencies
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the suitability of cryptocurrency for a client's core retirement savings, according to NASAA investor guidance?
options: Suitable, because digital assets are uncorrelated with stocks and insured.
Suitable for conservative investors seeking stable income.
Generally unsuitable — extremely risky speculation with a high risk of loss and no income.
Suitable only if purchased through a bank, which guarantees the principal.
questions.explanation: NASAA characterizes crypto investing as extremely risky speculation unsuitable for most long-term savings and retirement goals; investors should be prepared to lose everything.
why: They produce no income and are highly volatile.

questions.front: DPP flow-through: what passes through, and what can passive losses offset?
questions.back: Income, gains, losses, deductions, credits pass to investors (no dividends). Passive losses offset only passive income. LP max loss = investment + unpaid commitments.

questions.front: GP vs. LP: liability, management, minimum interest
questions.back: GP: manages, unlimited liability, ≥1% interest, fiduciary (no borrowing/competing/commingling). LP: passive, limited liability — managing risks losing it. Investors sign a subscription agreement.

questions.front: ETN vs. ETF registration; ETN key risk
questions.back: ETN: 1933 Act, unsecured debt, no underlying assets held → credit risk (plus liquidity, call, conflicts). ETF: 1940 Act investment company.

questions.front: Why are leveraged/inverse ETFs unsuitable for buy-and-hold?
questions.back: They reset daily — long-period results diverge from the index. Short horizons only. Principal-protected notes = zero-coupon + derivative; protection depends on issuer credit.

questions.front: Viatical vs. life settlement (no longer tested)
questions.back: Viatical: terminal, ≤24 months to live, any age. Life settlement: 65+, healthy, ≥2 years. Both are securities per NASAA.

questions.front: Passive real estate investments (no longer tested)
questions.back: REITs, real estate limited partnerships, stock of real estate companies. Active = managing or flipping property yourself.
Precious: gold, silver, platinum. Industrial: aluminum, nickel, copper, lead, tin. Most-traded commodity: crude oil.
Liquidity (greatest), legislative (tax-law change), audit, depreciation recapture.

questions.front: Commodity benefits / risks; structured product risks
questions.back: Benefits: inflation hedge, diversification, returns. Risks: volatility, foreign risks, leverage, no income. Structured: illiquid, mature-dependent, credit risk, inefficient pricing.

questions.front: Digital assets: three things they are NOT (NASAA)
questions.back: Not government-backed, not insured (FDIC/SIPC), not legal tender. Control via private key; hacks often unrecoverable; ICOs may be unregistered securities; 'extremely risky speculation.'

terms.def: A DPP structured for tax avoidance without economic purpose; IRS disallows deductions and assesses penalties.
Taxation of gain on sale above an asset's depreciated basis, possibly at ordinary rates.
Unsecured exchange-traded debt with an index-linked return; registered under the 1933 Act.
Daily published value of an ETN used by the issuer to manage issuance and redemption.
Fund seeking the opposite of its benchmark's daily return; may also be leveraged.
Sale of a life policy by an insured 65+ in reasonable health (no longer tested).
Document a DPP investor signs disclosing net worth and income and appointing the GP as agent.
Sale of a life policy by a terminally ill insured with ≤24 months to live (no longer tested).
Secret code controlling a digital asset wallet; loss or theft usually means permanent loss (external).
